etymology: Antioch toward Pisidia, a city of the highlands of Asia Minor, to be distinguished from the greater Antioch in Syria; the place of Paul’s first recorded sermon on his first journey.
biblical_def: Antioch in Pisidia is a city of the uplands of Asia Minor, set apart in the record from that other and greater Antioch in Syria whence Paul and Barnabas were sent. Hither they came on the first missionary journey: “when they departed from Perga, they came to Antioch in Pisidia, and went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and sat down” (Act 13:14). Here Paul preached his first sermon set down at length, rehearsing the history of Israel and preaching Jesus and the resurrection, until “the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed” (Act 13:48). So at this city the gospel turned plainly to the nations, and sovereign grace was seen in its saving: not all who heard, but as many as were ordained to life. Yet the unbelieving Jews raised persecution and thrust the apostles out. Let the believer see both truths at Pisidian Antioch: that the word of the Lord is published abroad and cannot be bound, and that they believe it who are appointed of God to eternal life, to the praise of the glory of His grace.

etymology: A seaport of Mysia in Asia Minor, on the coast opposite Lesbos; the town to which Paul went afoot alone while his companions sailed round the cape.
biblical_def: Assos is a seaport of Mysia on the western coast of Asia Minor, over against the isle of Lesbos. It has one memorable moment in the Scriptures, on Paul’s last voyage toward Jerusalem: his companions took ship and “sailed unto Assos, there intending to take in Paul: for so had he appointed, minding himself to go afoot” (Act 20:13). While the others rounded the headland by sea, the apostle chose to walk the shorter road by land, alone, and met them at Assos, whence “we took him in, and came to Mitylene” (Act 20:14). A small thing, yet it opens a window on the man: pressing toward Jerusalem though bonds awaited him, he took his solitary walk along the shore, perhaps to be alone with his God before the parting and the suffering to come. Let the believer mark the wisdom of it. There are stretches of the way the servant of God must walk afoot and alone, communing with his Master, before he takes ship again into the storm. Such solitary walks are not lost time but the very strengthening of the soul for what lies ahead.

etymology: The chief city of the isle of Lesbos in the Aegean Sea; a night’s anchorage on Paul’s last voyage toward Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Mitylene is the chief city of Lesbos, an isle of the Aegean, and served as one stage in the swift homeward voyage of Paul toward Jerusalem. Having taken the apostle in at Assos, the company “came to Mitylene” (Act 20:14), and from thence, day by day, they pressed on: “we sailed thence, and came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus” (Act 20:15). Mitylene is one of those quiet names that mark the ordinary stages of a journey — a harbour for the night, a place to lie at anchor before the next day’s sail. The Scriptures do not disdain to record them, for the LORD who directs the great turnings of a life also numbers its ordinary days and stages. Let the believer take comfort in the Mitylenes of his own pilgrimage: the unremarkable resting-places, the harbours of a single night, the days that seem only to pass. They too are appointed. They that go down to the sea in ships see the works of the LORD not only in the tempest but in the quiet anchorage, and every stage of the voyage is ordered by His hand.

etymology: A mountainous isle of the northern Aegean Sea; the first anchorage of Paul’s company as the gospel crossed from Asia into Europe.
biblical_def: Samothracia is a high and mountainous isle of the northern Aegean, and it holds an honour beyond its size: it was the first resting-place of the gospel as it crossed from Asia into Europe. Called by the vision of the man of Macedonia — “Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Act 16:9) — Paul and his company loosed from Troas: “we came with a straight course to Samothracia, and the next day to Neapolis” (Act 16:11). That night the ship lay under the shadow of the island’s peak, bearing the good news of Christ toward a continent that had never heard it. Here was a hinge of history, though the record is but a single verse: the westward march of the gospel that would in time reach Rome, and Britain, and the ends of the earth. Let the believer see the sovereign hand that steered that ship. The straight course to Samothracia was no chance of wind and tide, but the appointed path of the word of God going forth to conquer. The same LORD still sends His gospel where He will, and no sea is too wide, no continent too dark, for the advance of His saving truth.

etymology: A seaport of Lycia on the southern coast of Asia Minor; the harbour where Paul found a ship bound for Phenicia on his way to Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Patara is a seaport of Lycia on the southern coast of Asia Minor, a harbour of some trade in the Aegean and Mediterranean ways. On his last journey toward Jerusalem, Paul’s company came “unto Rhodes, and from thence unto Patara” (Act 21:1), and there the voyage took a decisive turn: “finding a ship sailing over unto Phenicia, we went aboard, and set forth” (Act 21:2). At Patara the coasting vessel was left behind and a larger ship taken for the open crossing to the east, toward the land where bonds and afflictions awaited the apostle. It is a picture of a threshold: the harbour where a man leaves the familiar shore-hugging way and commits himself to the deep for the sake of obedience. Paul knew what awaited him, for the Spirit witnessed in every city that bonds abided him; yet at Patara he went aboard and set forth. Let the believer learn the resolve of it. There are harbours in the life of faith where the safe and familiar course must be forsaken, and the soul must commit itself to the deep in plain obedience to God, counting not its life dear, that it may finish its course with joy.

etymology: A great isle and city of the south-eastern Aegean, famed among the nations; a day’s stage on Paul’s last voyage toward Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Rhodes is a large and famous isle of the south-eastern Aegean, renowned among the nations for its harbour and its great bronze colossus that once stood at its mouth, counted a wonder of the ancient world. Yet in the Scriptures it appears in a single humble clause of a traveller’s log: on the voyage to Jerusalem the company “came with a straight course unto Coos, and the day following unto Rhodes, and from thence unto Patara” (Act 21:1). The isle whose colossus men reckoned among the wonders of the world is named by the Holy Ghost only as a day’s stage in the journey of a bound apostle carrying the gospel of Christ. There is a quiet rebuke and a quiet glory in it. The proud monuments of men, their colossi and their fame, pass into a passing mention; but the errand of the servant of Christ, and the advance of the word he bore, are written in the Book that abides for ever. Let the believer measure greatness by another rule than the world’s. The wonders of Rhodes are dust; the gospel that sailed past it is the power of God unto salvation, and shall stand when every colossus is fallen.

etymology: A promontory and city at the south-western tip of Asia Minor; the point off which the contrary wind turned Paul’s ship toward Crete on the voyage to Rome.
biblical_def: Cnidus is a city set on a long promontory at the south-western tip of Asia Minor, where the Aegean meets the open Mediterranean. It marks a turning of Paul’s voyage to Rome, and a hard one: “when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete, over against Salmone” (Act 27:7). The contrary wind that would not let them hold their course drove the ship down under the lee of Crete — the first of the winds that would end in the great tempest and the shipwreck. Yet the same voyage was under an unbreakable promise, for the angel of God would stand by Paul and say, “Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar” (Act 27:24). Here is the mystery of providence at Cnidus: the wind blew against them, and yet the wind was in the hand of the God who had appointed the apostle to reach Rome. Let the believer learn that contrary winds are not the failure of God’s purpose but the servants of it. The gale that drives us from the course we chose is steering us, all the while, to the harbour He has appointed.

etymology: A seaport of Mysia in Asia Minor; the home port of the ship that first carried Paul as a prisoner toward Rome.
biblical_def: Adramyttium is a seaport of Mysia on the coast of Asia Minor, and it is remembered for the ship that bore its name. When Paul was delivered as a prisoner to be sent to Rome, the first vessel of the journey was “a ship of Adramyttium”: “entering into a ship of Adramyttium, we launched, meaning to sail by the coasts of Asia” (Act 27:2). It was a coasting vessel of that port, bound homeward along the shores of Asia, and it carried the apostle as far as Myra, where he was put aboard the Alexandrian ship that would meet the storm. There is a quiet providence in the naming. A common trading ship of Adramyttium, going about its ordinary business along the coast, was made the first stage in bringing the gospel’s ambassador to Caesar’s city. The LORD presses the ordinary commerce of the world into the service of His kingdom; the merchant’s ship, the trader’s route, the everyday sailing of men who knew nothing of God’s design, all bore Paul on toward Rome. Let the believer see how the LORD uses the common traffic of the world — its ships and roads and unwitting hands — to carry forward the errands of His grace.

etymology: An isle of the Aegean Sea off the coast of Ionia; a day’s stage on Paul’s swift voyage toward Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Chios is an isle of the Aegean lying off the Ionian coast of Asia Minor, over against Smyrna. It is named once, among the day-by-day stages of Paul’s hastening voyage toward Jerusalem: “we sailed thence, and came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus” (Act 20:15). The apostle was pressing homeward, “for he hasted, if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem the day of Pentecost” (Act 20:16), and Chios was one of the swift steps of that eager journey — a night over against the island, and on again with the next day’s light. The reckoning of the days is itself a testimony: the Spirit counts them out, one by one, “the next day… the next day.” The LORD numbers the stages of His servant’s haste as surely as the stations of his rest. Let the believer be diligent and eager in the work set before him, redeeming the time and pressing toward the mark; yet let him know that even his hastening is measured out by God, day by appointed day, and not one of them is wasted or unwatched.

etymology: An isle of the Aegean Sea off the coast of Ionia, near Ephesus; a day’s stage on Paul’s voyage toward Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Samos is an isle of the Aegean lying close to the Ionian coast, near Ephesus and over against the promontory of Mycale, by which runs the strait of Trogyllium. It is named among the day-by-day stages of Paul’s homeward voyage: “the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus” (Act 20:15). At Miletus, close beyond Samos, the apostle would send for the elders of Ephesus and take his last farewell of them, warning them with tears to feed the flock of God over which the Holy Ghost had made them overseers. So Samos is the last isle before that solemn parting — the quiet stage before the weeping on the shore. They that go down to the sea in ships, says the psalm, “these see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:24). The wonders are not only the tempests but the tender providences: the safe passage from isle to isle, the ordered days, the appointed meeting with beloved brethren just beyond the next headland. Let the believer trust the God who brings him, stage by stage, to the very partings and duties He has appointed, and who orders even the last quiet isle before the tears.
